asDecan.p: Each sign is split into three ten-degree slices called decans, each with a planet and a small card. Your Sun sits between 10 and 19 degrees of Gemini, the middle slice, where the sign is at full strength, and the Chaldean order gives it to Mars. Mars has no special dignity in Gemini. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, so it picks up the tone of Mercury, who owns the sign. You end up with Mercury's quick mind carrying Mars's urge to have a go, and because Gemini is air the fighting mostly happens in words and inside your own head. The slice before yours is the Eight of Swords, Jupiter's, where the mind talks itself into a corner. The one after is the Ten, the Sun's, where a story gets brought to its end. Yours has the most push of the three. Have a look at the person in the picture, sitting bolt upright in bed with their face in their hands. The Lovers is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You argue with people in the shower. Rehearsals, mostly, the thing you should have said in Tuesday's meeting, and by the time you're drying off you've won. At a family dinner someone makes a slightly off remark about your job or your politics and you let it go, and then you're still answering them in the car on the way home. A text left on read gets four or five readings from you, each one a bit worse than the last. You're quick in company and people like that about you, the joke lands before anyone else has thought of it. The trouble is the same engine keeps running after everyone leaves. A Sunday with nothing planned is harder for you than a busy one, because an idle Mars in an air sign goes looking for something to take on, and if there's nothing outside it'll find something inside.

The gift nobody expects from someone who worries this much is how good you are when something actually goes wrong. You've already run the bad version in your head, plenty of times, so when the phone call comes, the car dies on the motorway, a friend ends up in A&E, you're oddly calm. You know who to ring and what to ask. Mars much prefers a real fight to an imagined one, and a real problem finally gives all that nervous energy somewhere useful to go. There's another side to it as well. In a meeting where everyone is thinking the awkward thing, you're usually the one who says it, clearly and without much fuss, because Mercury gives you the words and Mars gives you the nerve. People who sit near you at work count on that more than they'd admit.

The less obvious shadow is that the worry doesn't always stay inside you. When you're wound up about something you can't fix, the money, a parent's health, a result you're waiting on, you tend to find something smaller to argue about instead. Your partner stacked the dishwasher wrong. A colleague's email had a tone. You go at it with a precision that's out of all proportion, and while it's happening it feels perfectly reasonable. Mars needs a target, and a nervous Gemini mind will hand it whatever is nearest. The other part of it is that worrying can feel like work. Going over a problem for the ninth time gives you the sense of doing something, and it's easy to lose a whole evening that way and still not make the one phone call that would settle it.

Bad news goes straight to your head. A redundancy, a break-up, a test result you're waiting on, and within the hour you've looked up everything there is to look up and read the worst forums on the internet. In those first days you talk about it a lot, to anyone, fast and a bit too bright. Then about a week in the talking stops and the nights get bad. You're awake at two going over it, tired and snappy by day, and the people around you get the short answers and the sharp edge without knowing why, because by then you've stopped explaining. What actually helps is physical. Mars has to go somewhere, and a hard walk, a swim or a run does more for this decan than another conversation at midnight. After that, say the specific fear out loud to one person, in daylight.

With The Lovers as your Sun card, relationships matter a great deal to you, and this slice adds a need to talk everything through, sometimes past the point where talking helps. You tend to like a partner who argues back. A bit of sparring over dinner feels like closeness, and someone who agrees with everything leaves you oddly restless. It gets harder when you're insecure. Then you read the relationship like a contract, the gap between texts, the single word ok with a full stop after it, the way they said goodnight, and you quietly build a case. Now and then you put that case to them at eleven at night, which almost never goes well. The people who suit you are steady and not easily rattled by a sharp word. It helps a lot to agree between you that nothing serious gets raised after ten.

You're good at anything that needs a quick mind and a bit of nerve. Work with an argument in it suits you, law, journalism, sales, negotiation, editing someone else's case until it holds up, fixing a system that's fallen over at the worst possible moment. You spot the weak point in a plan fast, and you'll say so in the meeting. That's useful, and it also puts some people on the defensive, so it's worth learning which things to raise one to one. Where you struggle is the waiting. A proposal sent off, a review booked for three weeks away, a restructure that's only a rumour. With nothing to act on, Mars turns the waiting into dread, and you can lose more sleep over an unanswered email than over a genuine crisis. Jobs with a steady supply of real problems are kinder to you than quiet ones.

At twenty this decan often looks like a lot of nervous energy without a clear aim. Late nights, strong opinions, long arguments online with strangers, sleep that goes to pieces around exams or a break-up, and a feeling that your own head is the loudest thing in any room. By the mid-thirties most people with a Sun here have learnt something about their own wiring. They know the bad thoughts come at night and count for less than the daytime ones, and they've usually found some physical outlet that keeps Mars occupied. The sharpness gets pointed at work and at things worth fighting for. The fifties tend to bring a hard-won sort of calm. People in these degrees often become the friend others ring at midnight, because they know that territory well and it doesn't frighten them much anymore.

Keep a notebook and a pen by the bed. When you wake in the night with something going round, write the one specific fear in a single sentence, and next to it the one thing you could actually do about it, with the day you'll do it. Then shut the notebook and put it face down. In the morning, read it before you look at your phone. Most mornings the sentence looks smaller than it felt. On the mornings it doesn't, the first step is already written down.
